newsitem.title: USA: Clinton's Asia trip seen as second-term model.
newsitem.headline: Clinton's Asia trip seen as second-term model.

text.p: President Bill Clinton's trip to Australia and Asia mixed work and play while producing some results and will probably become a model for his second-term foreign travel.

Notoriously averse to do-nothing holidays -- unlike most of his recent predecessors, he seldom visits Camp David because he considers the Maryland mountain hideaway too isolated -- Clinton could point to accomplishments on the 12-day trip from which he returned home early on Wednesday.

But he did get in some pure fun-in-the-sun with golf and snorkeling in Hawaii and Australia to help recover from the rigours of his re-election campaign. That included a close-up look at a giant clam on the Great Barrier Reef.
On the personal business side he conferred with the leaders of strategic allies Australia and Thailand and worked on trade policy at the Asian Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in the Philippines.

The Asian trade summit brought APEC's strong endorsement of a U.S.-led campaign for zero tariffs on computers and telecommunications equipment by the year 2000, which experts say could give the $1.8 trillion U.S. high tech industry an enormous boost.

"Information technology is the big growth area in the U.S. economy. This will mean new markets worldwide and new high-tech jobs at home," said Ambassador John Wolf, the Clinton administration's APEC coordinator.

On the fringes of the summit, Clinton sealed an agreement with Chinese President Jiang Zemin for reciprocal state visits over the next two years, although they continued to disagree over human rights, nuclear non-proliferation, Taiwan, trade and other issues.
These diplomatic plans, which include a visit to China by Vice President Al Gore early next year, signal the end of a long period of estrangement between Washington and Beijing.
Clinton also made time for a Hawaiian luau, a moonlight cruise with his wife Hillary -- and more than 100 others -- on Australia's Sydney Harbour, and sightseeing in Bangkok.

Even so, Clinton, a classic workaholic, drove himself so hard that his voice was shot by the time he left Thailand, the last stop on the trip. "I'll shut up for a few days (over the Thanksgiving holiday at the seldom-visited Camp David) and I'll be fine," he told reporters in a hoarse croak on the flight back to Washington.

"You're likely to see a lot more of (this kind of trip) over the next four years. The structure worked well for him," a top White House official said midway through the 20,000-mile trip, referring to the fact that the president took time for relaxation between bouts of diplomacy.

Clinton, who criticised George Bush for his foreign travel during the 1992 presidential campaign, wound up globetrotting even more than Bush in his first term -- although many of his trips were one-day dashes to faraway places for an international conference or a visit with U.S. troops.

His second term is likely to see even more travel abroad, White House insiders say. Clinton's tentative 1997 schedule includes Latin America and Africa, a trip to Canada for the 1997 APEC forum and perhaps a visit to Greece and Turkey.

As a result of his meeting with Jiang in Manila, he will also visit China in 1997 or 1998. And before he leaves office in the year 2001, Clinton is also likely to visit New Zealand and Brunei, since they will host Asian trade summits in 1998 and 1999.
